newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Little Asia impact seen from 25 point US rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Little Asia impact seen from 25 point US rate rise.

text.p: Asian markets should escape much fallout from a 25 basis point increase in U.S. interest rates, but any sign that more than one increase is on the horizon could cause significant damage, HSBC Asset Management said on Tuesday.
"So long as it is a modest rise in rates, the impact on Asia should be fairly modest," said Ian Burden, chief investment officer for the Asia Pacific region.

"But obviously, if we get a further correction on Wall Street ... we could see some weakness in Hong Kong, especially given that it does have a strong correlation on the downside with Wall Street," Burden said.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the policy-making body of the U.S. Federal Reserve, is widely expected to raise U.S. interest rates by 25 basis points at a meeting later on Tuesday.

Wall Street has largely discounted a 25 basis point increase in the Federal funds rate, Burden said, but HSBC considers U.S. stocks at least six percent overbought at current levels and vulnerable to a correction.

Any sign that a series of rate hikes were in the works or that corporate earnings would fail to meet expectations of between 10 and 14 percent growth could spark a sell-off on Wall Street -- and across Asia.
Burden said so far, earnings disappointments have been restricted to individual stocks and sectors, prompting some "fairly aggressive" sector rotation.
"It's been stock specific so far, but if it becomes any more generalised it will be a worry for Wall Street beyond interest rates," Burden said.
Any correction on Wall Street will hurt Hong Kong, but HSBC Asset Management remains positive on the market in the meantime, which it considers attractive at current levels.

HSBC is expecting to see further consolidation in the crucial Hong Kong property stock sector, even though the market itself remains healthy and well-supported by strong demand and a structural shortage of supply over the next two years, said Hong Kong fund manager Man Wing Chung.

Across Asia, many economies are strong enough to cope with HSBC Asset Management's forecast of a 50 basis points rise in U.S. rates over the next 12 months, said Stella Yiu, director of Asian equities.
"However, if we see a series of multiple tightenings, that could be worrying insofar as equity markets in Asia are concerned," she said.
Rising interest rates are another concern for rate-sensitive markets in Asia, which are lagging Latin America and Eastern Europe in the race for emerging market investment.

Yiu said Latin America's turn to recovery after a two-year correction and a spectacular performance by markets in Eastern Europe, and Russia in particular, are giving Asian equities a run for their money.
Greater China, however, offers convincing opportunities through H shares and red chips in Hong Kong and B shares available to foreigners in Shanghai and Shenzhen, Yiu said.
"Greater China is still very interesting, but Hong Kong and Taiwan would not be as interesting as last year," she added.
